implementation_notes: The metadata store is the attribute definition object: each key is a model property and its options (type, field: 'user_name', allowNull, primaryKey, autoIncrement), with model options such as tableName beside it; Model.init (or sequelize.define, which calls it) registers the model with the Sequelize instance, which is the reader - it builds the model manager and derives SQL from the attribute list, so CRUD comes from the generic engine and no per-model mapping code exists. Table names, and the identifiers inside them, are inferred unless pinned (freezeTableName, tableName, field), which is a convention layer over the explicit metadata. Reach for query builders or raw SQL when a query cannot be expressed through the model API.
pitfalls: Public class fields with the same name as an attribute shadow the accessors Sequelize generates; in TypeScript such properties must be declared with the declare keyword.
Definition order and imports matter: a model or association registered after it is used, or dropped by a circular import, silently loses its mapping.
Attributes not declared are ignored on create, so a database column missing from the definition disappears from writes without an error.

variants.name: Mongoose Schema definition + model()
variants.implementation_notes: For document stores the same shape appears as a Schema object whose keys declare every path with type and options (required, default, index, ref); mongoose.model() compiles it into the Model used for reads and writes. The schema is the metadata store and the library is reader and engine: it casts input to the declared types, applies validators and defaults, tracks modified paths and generates the queries, so again no per-class mapping code exists. Choose it when the store is MongoDB and the mapping problem is document shape rather than table/column correspondence; the path names double as the stored field names, so renaming a schema key changes the stored data unless the schema is versioned.
pitfalls: Schemas are enforced on write by casting and stripping: strict mode drops unknown fields, so legacy documents lose data unless strict/select are handled.
Changing the schema does not migrate documents: previously valid data can violate new required/default declarations when it is next read or written.
Index declarations in the schema were built automatically at startup, which is expensive in production and should be disabled and managed explicitly.
